blocks.prompt: The Bird That Flies Underwater
blocks.text: A puffin spends most of its life far out on the open sea. It sleeps on the waves. It only comes to land in spring, to make a nest. A puffin digs a burrow in the dirt on top of a cliff. It uses its beak and its feet. Inside the burrow, the mother puffin lays one egg. Just one. Both parents sit on the egg and keep it warm. When the chick hatches, it is called a puffling. The parents fly out to sea and bring back small fish. A puffin can carry lots of fish in its beak at once.

blocks.prompt: Two Ways to Fly
blocks.text: Most birds fly through the air. The puffin flies through both. In the air, a puffin has to beat its wings about four hundred times a minute just to stay up. It looks like a windup toy. Under the water, everything changes. The puffin folds its wings in and flaps them like short paddles, and suddenly it is graceful. It can dive deeper than a house is tall and stay under for half a minute, chasing small silver fish called sand eels. Catching one fish is easy. Carrying ten is the trick. The roof of a puffin's mouth is lined with tiny spines that point backward. The puffin holds the fish it has already caught against those spines with its tongue, then opens its beak and catches another. The fish hang crosswise, all in a neat row, and none of them slip out. A puffin's bright beak is not permanent. After the summer, the colorful outer plates fall off, and the puffin spends the winter at sea with a smaller, duller beak.

blocks.prompt: The Puffling Patrol
blocks.text: On a summer night in the Westman Islands, off the south coast of Iceland, children go out with flashlights and cardboard boxes. They are not playing. They are on patrol. Iceland is puffin country. More Atlantic puffins nest there than anywhere else on Earth, packed into burrows in the grassy slopes above the sea. Each pair raises a single chick, called a puffling, in a tunnel under the turf. The parents feed it fish for about six weeks. Then they stop. Hungry and alone, the puffling waits until dark and walks out of the burrow for the first and last time. It has never seen the ocean. It has never flown. It heads for the brightest thing on the horizon, which for millions of years was moonlight on the water, and it launches itself off the cliff toward the sea. But the Westman Islands have a town now, and the town has streetlights. Every year some pufflings steer toward the lamps instead of the moon and end up flapping around a parking lot, lost, in danger from cars and cats and gulls. So the children come out. They scoop the birds up, keep them safe overnight in boxes, and in the morning they carry them to the shore, lift them into the wind, and let them go. The birds do the rest themselves. A young puffin will not touch land again for two or three years. It will sleep on the open ocean, riding the waves, until it is old enough to come back and dig a burrow of its own.

5.title: The Bird That Flies Underwater
5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Fratercula arctica, the Atlantic puffin

One egg per pair, per year

blocks.prompt: Built for the Open Ocean
blocks.text: The Atlantic puffin is a small bird, about the height of a soda can, and almost everything about it is a solution to the same problem: how do you live on the open ocean? Start with the drinking water. There isn't any. A puffin spends eight months of the year hundreds of miles from land, surrounded by water it cannot safely drink. So it drinks it anyway. Above each eye sits a salt gland, a filter that pulls the salt out of the bloodstream and drips it back out through the nostrils. The bird carries its own desalination plant in its skull. Then the flying. A puffin's wings are a compromise, and a bad one on paper. They are too small for its body, so it must beat them roughly four hundred times a minute to stay airborne, and it lands like a thrown shoe. But those same short, stiff wings are superb underwater. A puffin does not paddle. It flies down through the sea, wings beating, steering with its feet, and it can reach depths of sixty meters and hold its breath for a minute. Then the famous beak. It is a billboard and a tool at once. In spring it swells into orange, blue, and yellow plates, and under ultraviolet light, which puffins can see and we cannot, parts of it glow. After the breeding season those outer plates simply fall away, and the bird spends winter with a plain gray beak that no tourist would photograph. The tool part is inside: backward-pointing spines on the roof of the mouth let the puffin pin caught fish with its tongue while it dives for more, which is how one small bird flies home with a dozen sand eels lined up crosswise. Puffins live a long time, often more than twenty years, and they are careful with it. A pair usually returns to the same burrow year after year and raises one chick a season. That is a slow way to build a population and a fast way to lose one. Warming seas have pushed sand eels away from some colonies, and parents that cannot find the right fish come back with substitutes their chick can barely swallow.

6.title: The Bird That Flies Underwater
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Fratercula arctica, family Alcidae, the auks
Water is about 800 times denser than air
Its flightless cousin, the great auk, died out in 1844
Dives to around 60 meters, wings beating
Salt glands above the eyes filter seawater
One egg a year, fed for about six weeks

blocks.prompt: The Compromise: Why the Puffin Flies Badly on Purpose
blocks.text: A puffin in flight looks like a mistake. It is a stocky, football-shaped bird with wings too short for its weight, and it stays in the air only by beating them around four hundred times a minute. It cannot glide. It cannot hover. It approaches its own cliff at fifty miles an hour and arrives more or less by crashing. Watch one land and the obvious conclusion is that evolution simply got this bird wrong. It did not. The puffin is not a bad flier. It is a compromise, and the compromise is deliberate. Puffins belong to a family of seabirds called auks, and auks make their living underwater. A wing that works well in air needs to be long and broad, because air is thin and you need a great deal of it to push against. A wing that works well underwater needs to be short and stiff, because water is roughly eight hundred times denser than air, and a long wing would stall or snap. No wing can be excellent at both. The auks chose the water. A puffin does not swim the way a duck does, kicking along the surface. It flies down into the sea, wings beating, feet trailing behind as rudders, and it can reach sixty meters below the surface, deeper than most divers ever go. Everything awkward about the puffin in the air is the price of that. The family took the trade further than the puffin did. The great auk, the puffin's much larger cousin, gave up flight altogether: a flightless, penguin-like bird about eighty-five centimeters tall that bred on remote North Atlantic islands. It was easy to catch, and it was caught. Sailors killed the last confirmed pair in Iceland in 1844. The puffin's clumsy half-measure, in other words, is also what saved it. A bird that can still fly can still nest on a clifftop no fox can climb. The rest of the puffin follows the same logic. It drinks seawater and filters the salt back out through glands above its eyes. It spends roughly eight months of the year out of sight of land, sleeping on the swell. Its bright beak, the part everyone photographs, is seasonal equipment: the colored plates grow in for the breeding season and drop off afterward, leaving a small, dull winter bill. Inside that beak, backward-facing spines on the palate let the bird hold a row of caught fish against its tongue while it dives for the next one, which is why a puffin comes home with a dozen sand eels crosswise in its bill instead of one. What the puffin cannot compromise on is food. A pair produces one egg a year, and both parents spend about six weeks ferrying fish to a chick sealed in a burrow. That strategy assumes something specific: that the right fish, at the right size, will be in the right water in the right week. Sand eels are that fish for most Atlantic colonies. As sea temperatures have risen, sand eels have shifted north and thinned out, and puffin parents have arrived at their burrows carrying whatever they could find instead. Some colonies have failed to raise chicks for years running. The bird that solved the ocean by refusing to specialize in flight is now in trouble over the one thing it did specialize in. The puffin looks like a joke and works like an engineer. The joke was never on the bird.
